events.description: AQAP formation announced by a quartet of al-Qaeda veterans including Wuhayshi, stating goal of emirate leading to caliphate.
Fort Hood shooting by Nidal Hasan, influenced by Awlaki's teachings (host gives 2009).
Failed Christmas Day underwear bomb attempt by Abdulmutallab, guided personally by Awlaki.
Anwar al-Awlaki killed in U.S. drone strike.
Two AQAP brothers stormed Charlie Hebdo office in Paris (hosts said January 2011 in intro, likely misstatement).
Batarfi freed from Mukalla prison when AQAP overran the city; then appeared in rallies as featured speaker.
Qasim al-Raymi takes over as AQAP emir after Wuhayshi is killed and reaffirms bayah to Zawahiri.
Taliban video celebrating Taliban–al-Qaeda bond featured Batarfi praising Mullah Omar.
Pensacola NAS shooting by Saudi trainee al-Shamrani; three Americans killed, eight wounded; AQAP later claimed it.
Qasim al-Raymi killed in U.S. drone strike before AQAP's Pensacola claim video appeared.
U.S.–Taliban withdrawal deal signed (about three-plus weeks before episode); Taliban has conducted zero raids on al-Qaeda since.
Khalid Batarfi named new AQAP emir and swears oath to Zawahiri; praises Taliban deal in first audio message.
Ibrahim al-Banna dispatched to Yemen in early 1990s to build tribal ties for bin Laden and Zawahiri.
Ibrahim al-Qosi repatriated from Guantanamo to Sudan under plea deal during Obama administration (host says 'several years ago').
Only one or two US air strikes in Yemen last year.
Khalid Batarfi named new AQAP emir; some chatter about his nomination reported in Arab press.

key_claims: AQAP leadership is integrated into al-Qaeda's senior management, undermining the 'core vs. affiliate' dichotomy.
Wuhayshi was both AQAP emir and al-Qaeda's general manager.
Batarfi was groomed for leadership, trained at Al-Farouq, fought with Taliban and is a long-time al-Qaeda ideologue.
Taliban has conducted zero raids or statements against al-Qaeda or AQIS since the U.S. deal, and Batarfi views the deal as a jihadist win.
Awlaki directly planned and directed plots (Abdulmutallab, Karim, Pham) rather than just inspiring.
Ansar al-Sharia is an AQAP front used to ease Sharia in and win local support.
AQAP retains the bigger footprint in Yemen over ISIS, cooperating or clashing as convenient.
AQAP's resilience stems from insurgent structure, depth of veteran leaders like al-Qosi and al-Banna, and ideology.
Al-Qaeda branches such as AQAP, Shabab and AQIM aim to build emirates, starting locally and thinking globally.
AQAP learned from Iraq's backlash to ease Sharia in gradually and avoid alienating local populations.
AQAP avoided showing atrocities like stonings and advertised public services in Mukalla to build support.
Decapitation strikes are necessary but not sufficient to defeat al-Qaeda affiliates because of their deep benches.
No AQAP commanders have broken away or defected to ISIS since Batarfi's naming, though internal dissent is possible.
